title: Computing Power for Reasoning in the Agent Era: Where Are GPU, HBM, and Compute Chip Funds Flowing?
excerpt: Agents are shifting the competition in AI chips from individual chips to entire systems. This article breaks down the sources of profit for cloud platforms, data centers, GPUs, HBM, and advanced packaging by examining a specific task, and it also looks at how contracts and financing can accelerate development, considering edge AI as a second demand curve that needs to be verified.
body: The way Agents work is shifting the competition in AI chips from individual chips to entire systems. An Agent plans steps, invokes tools, reads results, and then proceeds with further reasoning. With each step taken, the model may need to reprocess the context, read from and write to the KV Cache, and utilize computing, memory, and network resources. Therefore, compared to token consumption, what is more important to track currently is the **Effective Token Ratio** and the **cost per inference call required to achieve a certain level of value**. Agents will continue to drive demand for cloud-based inference, and this demand will also spread upstream to GPU, HBM, advanced packaging, servers, networks, power supply, and liquid cooling solutions. Profits will not be evenly distributed across all these areas of expansion. Those that have a better chance of gaining higher profits are those that either possess scarce production capacity, high yield rates, and customer certifications, or can integrate chips, software scheduling, and customer billing into a stable delivery system. At the same time, long-term contracts, upfront payments, and debt financing turn future usage expectations into current investments in data centers and equipment. Once demand falls below the assumptions made during procurement, pressure will first show up in price signals such as rental costs, with utilization rates and asset returns reflecting these changes later on. The edge side represents a second demand curve. Automotive and home devices indeed require lower latency, offline functionality, and on-device data processing, but this curve still needs to be validated through factors such as usage frequency, device cost, and product margin. The cloud sector is already in a phase of large-scale development, while the edge side remains more of a concept that awaits validation through actual product performance. ## Agents turn task completion into a new cost factor Typical question-answering interactions involve only one round of input and output. An Agent, however, breaks down a goal into multiple steps, invokes external tools, retrieves results, and then decides on the next step. A single task may involve multiple rounds of model invocation, with different steps requiring models of varying sizes. The total cost is determined by the number of invocations, the length of the context, the cache hit rate, and the number of retry attempts. Inference using large models typically involves Prefill and Decode phases. Prefill processes the already provided input, allowing for parallel computation. Decode generates new tokens one by one, requiring repeated access to model weights and the previously generated KV Cache, making it more susceptible to memory bandwidth limitations. As the context length increases, the amount of space occupied by the KV Cache also rises with the batch size and sequence length. In such cases, the peak computing capacity remains important, while memory capacity, bandwidth, inter-card communication, and scheduling efficiency directly affect throughput. I will use the following comparison to illustrate the differences between various inference systems. ```text Cost per million valid tokens = Total system cost per hour ÷ Valid tokens generated per hour × 1,000,000 ``` The total cost of a complete system includes accelerators, HBM, servers, networking infrastructure, power supply, liquid cooling systems, software, hosting services, and depreciation. The effective number of tokens generated per hour needs to be calculated under fixed model parameters, average input and output lengths, concurrency levels, as well as specific requirements regarding latency and quality. Results resulting from queue timeouts, failed retries, or those that do not meet quality standards should not be counted as part of the output. Input tokens, output tokens, and cache hits also need to be recorded separately. Only when the cost per task decreases can tasks that previously could not cover the costs associated with model invocation, software integration, and manual oversight become feasible for inclusion in a product. Further reductions in price may lead to an increase in usage. However, such growth is contingent on both high task completion rates and high value of the results. Simply generating more tokens will only increase equipment usage without necessarily creating sustainable demand. ## How an Agent Task Contributes to Infrastructure Profitability A chargeable task first generates demands for model invocation and context processing, which in turn lead to the need for computing power, memory, networking capabilities, and data center resources. The diagram below illustrates these layers of demand transmission, the secondary curve related to end-user operations, and financial risks. Moving from left to right, the stages closer to the user make it easier to manage scheduling and billing, while those further upstream rely more on production capacity, quality levels, and certification to establish bargaining power. ```html ``` **GPUs, ASICs, and Software Stack** The profitability of GPUs stems from their versatility, mature software ecosystems, and ability to quickly adapt to new models. Even as model architectures and request patterns continue to evolve, customers can use the same hardware and tools for training, development, and various inference tasks, keeping migration costs relatively manageable. ASICs allow for cost and energy efficiency optimization by being tailored to specific models, precision levels, and consistent request patterns. Their economic viability depends on three conditions: sufficient workload volume to cover the costs of chip development and deployment, software that can integrate existing customer models, operators, and maintenance processes. For example, AWS combines Trainium with its Neuron software stack, servers, networking infrastructure, and cloud services into one comprehensive product suite, while Google uses TPUs, networking solutions, and Pathways to support large-scale inference. These examples show that the competitive unit for specialized chips has expanded to include entire systems. It’s difficult to determine whether a chip can generate sustained profits based solely on its theoretical performance. **HBM and Advanced Packaging** Long contexts and concurrent requests increase memory usage for weights and KV caches, while decoding requires continuous data transfer. As a result, the capacity and bandwidth of HBM affect the utilization rate of accelerators. Advanced packaging is responsible for combining computing chips with multiple HBM modules, while also meeting requirements related to quality, power consumption, and customer certifications. When supply is limited in the short term, suppliers who can consistently deliver qualified products are more likely to command higher prices. There are clear conditions under which these premium prices may decline. New production capacity comes online, quality improves, alternative solutions gain certification, or customers start diversifying their suppliers, thereby reducing the bargaining power resulting from supply constraints (for example, with the emergence of companies like GigaDevice). As of September 2026, TSMC has raised its annual capital expenditure target to between $60 billion and $64 billion, attributing this to customer-driven demand for increased production. SK hynix has announced that HBM4 production began in the second quarter of 2026, with further increases planned for the second half of the year, and the company has already signed long-term agreements with around ten key customers. While these announcements indicate growing demand and expansion efforts, they do not guarantee that current premium prices will persist in the long term. **Servers, Networking, Power Supply, and Liquid Cooling** GPUs and HBM can only become deployable computing resources when installed in servers, connected to low-latency networks, and supplied with stable power. Google provides its Ironwood system with liquid cooling capable of handling up to 9,216 chips, resulting in a system power consumption of nearly 10 MW. Although this example does not represent all server clusters, it shows that procurement considerations now extend beyond just the chips themselves. Profitability in these areas typically comes from factors such as access to power, delivery speed, system integration, and reliability. These areas also involve longer construction periods and higher capital investments. Even after a data center is built, depreciation, maintenance costs, and power contracts continue to apply. Revenue can grow rapidly with new construction orders, but capital returns depend on whether equipment is deployed on schedule, whether utilization rates meet expectations, and whether contracts cover the asset recovery period. **Scheduling Software and Cloud Platforms** Cloud providers control access points for customers, model deployment, task routing, and billing. Scheduling software can improve batch processing efficiency, reuse caches, reduce idle time and failed retries, allowing the same hardware to handle more tasks. Cloud platforms can also distribute workloads between GPUs and custom ASICs, translating changes in hardware costs into adjustments to customer prices or platform margins. Profitability in this area depends on customer usage levels, software compatibility, and migration costs, and it is also affected by price competition and capital expenditures. Only when cloud providers increase their equipment purchases and see corresponding increases in task revenue and cash flow can their operational advantages translate into sustainable profits. ## Financing Enables Earlier Supply Development Than Actual Revenue Generation AI infrastructure requires a long procurement and construction timeline. Cloud providers plan computing capacity based on customer demands, GPU cloud service providers build data centers according to contracts, and server, memory, and packaging manufacturers expand production based on orders. Each stage relies on early procurement signals, but it often takes until the equipment is deployed to determine whether end-users will continue to pay. In the second-quarter 2026 earnings call, TSMC’s management mentioned that while the demands submitted by customers may be legitimate, further evaluation is still needed after summing up all these requests. The company also monitors the progress of data center construction, location selection, and rack setup to avoid inventory buildup after chips are delivered. This indicates that upstream manufacturers are aware of the gap between orders and actual deployment. At the same time, NVIDIA is collaborating with financial institutions to package chips as financial assets and use them to invest in small startups. By doing so, it not only increases its own sales but also indirectly supports investment in cutting-edge technologies while establishing strong partnerships. These startups are required to continue purchasing chips from NVIDIA on a periodic basis according to agreed terms and demands. Alternatively, Meta has established shell companies to participate in data center construction. Although this does not affect the parent company’s financial results on paper, such financial engineering practices could have disruptive effects if industry conditions deteriorate or other uncertainties arise. Both approaches rely on the same mechanism: financing shifts the decision-making timeline forward and transfers risks away from decision-makers. When cloud providers and GPU cloud service providers purchase equipment, the assets and depreciation are recorded on their balance sheets, while debts and leasing obligations remain fixed. Once the equipment is deployed, depreciation, power costs, and interest continue to accrue, regardless of whether tasks are being processed. The only things that can be postponed are payments, depending on whether end-users are willing to continue paying. Purchase orders are then sent down through the same chain, layer by layer. Cloud service providers allocate computing power according to the contracts, GPU cloud service providers build data centers based on those contracts, and server, memory, and packaging manufacturers expand production in response to these orders. Each layer receives definite signals from the layer above; no single layer can see the total actual usage across all layers. Contracts convert expected usage over several years into orders today, and the combined supply from these orders may exceed current demand. While each layer’s assessment seems valid on its own, the total might still exceed actual usage. None of these phenomena prove that a bubble has formed, but they consistently indicate that leverage is increasing. They show that long-term contracts and financing can convert future revenue into servers, GPUs, and data centers today. As valid workloads continue to grow, building in advance can shorten delivery times and improve asset utilization. Even if demand growth, renewal rates, or utilization fall short of procurement assumptions, costs such as leasing, depreciation, electricity, and interest will still persist. Pressure does not appear across all metrics simultaneously nor is it evenly distributed. Even if the total amount of work processed by models continues to rise, as long as supply grows faster, price-related indicators will be affected first, including GPU rental prices, residual values of used devices, server inventory, and certain memory prices. Utilization and renewal rates are operational outcomes that lag behind; asset returns become apparent only after a full cycle of depreciation and interest. Suppliers may continue to receive orders before end-demand slows down, until a point is reached where new revenue is no longer sufficient to cover capital costs. At that point, the financial amplification effect will work in reverse, creating a bullwhip effect. ## The edge side is the second curve awaiting validation through actual usage Car assistants and home control hubs need to respond quickly and still be able to perform certain tasks in low-network conditions. Information about vehicle status, home sensors, and personal habits involves privacy concerns, so local processing can reduce the amount of data that needs to be uploaded. The edge side is well-suited for tasks such as activation, sensing, simple decision-making, and frequent control, while complex reasoning and long-context processing can remain in the cloud. Local processing consumes power from the user’s device, so manufacturers still have to bear upfront costs. Higher-specification SoCs, memory, and storage increase the bill of materials, and engineering resources are needed for cooling, model adaptation, security, OTA updates, and long-term after-sales support. Manufacturers will only continue to bear these costs in the long term if local inference can enable higher prices, reduce cloud usage expenses, improve the user experience, or meet privacy and offline requirements. Edge chips must also handle model updates while operating with limited power consumption. Techniques such as low-bit computing, more efficient memory architectures, and edge-cloud scheduling can help overcome these limitations. The ability to deploy models does not necessarily mean there will be stable demand. The actual usage frequency of cars and home devices, the proportion of tasks handled locally, incremental hardware costs, and product gross margins remain the most important indicators for validating this curve. Once edge devices become more frequently used, demand will become more dispersed and better reflect users’ daily behavior. Current available information is not sufficient to prove that this stage has arrived, so I will consider it the second curve and avoid assuming large-scale chip orders at this point. ## What signals will I wait for? For cloud demand, I will look at the volume of paid tasks, task completion rates, and revenue per task. Effective tokens can help compare inference systems, but they need to be considered alongside latency, quality, and failure rates. Cloud providers’ capital expenditures must translate into revenue from AI cloud services, cash flow, and higher output per megawatt. For the supply chain, I will examine whether there is a divergence in prices and inventory levels between HBM and standard DRAM, whether the delivery times for advanced packaging are shortening, and whether GPU rental prices and residual values of used GPUs are starting to decline. Profits resulting from supply constraints only become sustainable advantages if manufacturers can maintain high yields, certification advantages, and customer loyalty even after expanding production. Regarding the financial structure, I will consider whether contract terms, debt maturities, and the economic lifespan of GPUs are aligned. Customer renewals, the progress of data center deployments, and utilization rates can help determine whether long-term contracts are locking in actual demand or simply bringing future demand into today’s investments. For the edge side, I will focus on the average daily usage of assistants, the proportion of tasks completed locally, and device gross margins. Only when cars and home devices start handling frequent tasks will demand for edge chips shift from competition over specifications to product capabilities that users are willing to use consistently. If valid workloads and revenue can keep up with computing power supply, there is still room for expansion in GPUs, ASICs, HBM, packaging, and data centers. Profits will primarily accrue to those who can reduce costs per task, control limited supply, or manage customers and scheduling processes. When leading indicators such as rental prices and residual values continue to weaken, and utilization rates, renewals, and asset returns remain below procurement assumptions, even if the agent-based narrative still holds, expectations for infrastructure investment will need to be lowered. ## Key Sources - [NVIDIA Inference Optimization Guide](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/), Prefill, Decode, KV Cache, and memory bandwidth - [AWS Trainium Official Documentation](https://aws.amazon.com/ai/machine-learning/trainium/), system design for chips, Neuron software stack, servers, networks, and cloud services - [Google Ironwood Official Overview](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/infrastructure-and-cloud/google-cloud/ironwood-tpu-age-of-inference/), computing, memory, interconnection, and liquid cooling configurations for large-scale inference - [TSMC Q2 2026 Earnings Call](https://investor.tsmc.com/chinese/encrypt/files/encrypt_file/reports/2026-07/547d1696765e05ce3adb81c108ce1c8c1682b80c/TSMC+2Q26+Transcript.pdf), capital expenditures, expansion decisions, and end-market deployment status - [SK hynix Q2 2026 Earnings Report](https://news.skhynix.com/en/q2-2026-business-results), HBM4 shipments, long-term agreements, and expansion plans
